meta.name: E-Waste Recycling & Management
meta.definition: The industry covering collection, dismantling, recycling and resource recovery of end-of-life electrical and electronic equipment (computers, mobiles, TVs, appliances, batteries, solar panels) in India, spanning formal CPCB-authorised recyclers and the large informal/unorganised sector.

summary.headline: India's e-waste management market is valued at roughly USD 2-4 billion (estimates vary by methodology) in 2025-26 and growing at a double-digit CAGR, even as the country generates an estimated 3.8-6.2 million tonnes of e-waste a year but recycles only a small fraction through authorised, formal channels.
key_takeaways: India is the world's third-largest e-waste generator (after China and the US), producing an estimated 3.8-6.2 MMT annually, yet the informal sector still handles 60-90%+ of this volume with far lower material-recovery efficiency than formal recyclers.

Formal recycling capacity has roughly doubled since 2021 (1.1 to 1.8 million tonnes) and the CPCB-reported formal recycling rate has reportedly jumped from ~22% in 2019-20 to over 70% in 2024-25 on some measures, though independent estimates put the true formal share closer to 10-30%.

Metals (gold, silver, copper, aluminium, palladium) dominate the economics of recycling, contributing ~46% of material value and over 80% of recycler revenue despite being under 2% of e-waste mass; India is heavily import-dependent on these same critical minerals (100% for lithium, cobalt, rare earths).

Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 is the central regulatory lever, with collection targets rising from 60% (FY2023-24) to 80% (FY2027-28) and coverage expanded from 21 to 106 EEE categories, alongside new Battery Waste Management Rules for EV/Li-ion batteries.

Attero Recycling is the clear market leader with an estimated ~25% share of the organised sector, followed by Eco Recycling (Ecoreco), Cerebra Integrated Technologies, Re Sustainability and Namo eWaste; the market overall remains fragmented, with the top five firms controlling well under 20% of total industry revenue.
summary.report_markdown:
## Market size and growth
Estimates of India's e-waste management market size vary widely by methodology and scope: Mordor Intelligence pegs it at USD 1.88 billion (2025) rising to USD 2.02 billion (2026) and USD 2.87 billion by 2031 (7.3% CAGR); IMARC Group's broader scope estimates USD 3.32 billion (2025) growing to USD 4.14 billion (2026) and USD 9.95 billion by 2034 (11.6% CAGR); other houses place 2025 figures anywhere from USD 1.7 billion to USD 3.45 billion depending on whether allied services and full-value scrap are included. On the generation side, CPCB data shows India generated 13.97 lakh tonnes (~1.4 MMT) of e-waste in FY2024-25, while a separate NITI Aayog/REDSEER-style estimate puts actual generation far higher at ~6.19 MMT in 2024 (up from ~2.76 MMT in 2020), and Mordor Intelligence cites 3.8 million tonnes for FY24 — reflecting large definitional gaps between official collection-rule categories and total discarded-electronics volumes.

## Formal vs informal split - the core structural issue
Multiple sources agree that **India's e-waste economy is still dominated by an informal, unorganised sector** that handles anywhere from 60% to over 90% of volumes, achieving only 10-30% material recovery efficiency versus 95-97%+ in formal hydrometallurgical/pyrometallurgical plants. As of FY24, India had 595 authorised recyclers/dismantlers with combined capacity of ~1.8 MMT, concentrated heavily in Maharashtra (~25% of formal capacity), yet the informal sector still captures roughly 60%+ of the recoverable economic value from e-waste streams. CPCB-reported 'formal recycling rate' jumped from ~22% (2019-20) to over 70% (2024-25) by some industry counts, but other sources (REDSEER, Vision IAS) put India's true formal recycling rate at just ~10%, well below the global average of ~22% and far behind USA (56%) and EU countries (55%+).

## Segments
- **By material**: Metals lead with 45-46% share (gold, silver, copper, aluminium recovery economics), followed by Plastics (~20-28%), Glass (~15%, mainly CRT) and Others (~10%).
- **By source**: Consumer Electronics is the largest source category (37-40% share), followed by Industrial Electronics and Others (medical, industrial machinery, automotive electronics).
- **By application**: Recycled applications hold ~50% share versus Trashed, as formal infrastructure and EPR compliance expand.
- **By region**: West India leads with ~28-29% share (Maharashtra's manufacturing density + Gujarat's metallurgical clusters), followed by South India (~27%, Bengaluru/Hyderabad IT), North India (~26%, Delhi-NCR) and East India (~18%, emerging).

## Players
Attero Recycling is positioned as the clear market leader (~25% of the organised sector), with 4 recycling plants (Uttarakhand, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Haryana) and pan-India coverage; it has launched platforms like Selsmart (D2C take-back), Metal Mandi (scrap marketplace) and is scaling to ~244,000 tonnes/annum processing capacity. Other significant formal players include Eco Recycling Ltd (Ecoreco), Cerebra Integrated Technologies, Re Sustainability (Ramky), Namo eWaste Management (listed on NSE SME, oversubscribed IPO Sept 2024), Exigo Recycling, TES-AMM India, E-Parisaraa and RecycleKaro. Together Attero, Ecoreco and Cerebra are estimated to command 45-55% of organised-sector revenue. Globally, Umicore, Sims, Veolia and Boliden are referenced benchmarks for advanced hydrometallurgy/pyrometallurgy. Producer Responsibility Organisations (PROs) such as Karo Sambhav (clients include Apple, Dell, HP, Lenovo) and RLG India coordinate EPR compliance for major OEMs.

## Regulatory framework and India-specific context
The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 (effective 1 April 2023) replaced the 2016 framework, expanding coverage from 21 to 106 EEE categories and mandating EPR collection targets rising from 60% (FY2023-24) to 80% (FY2027-28). A parallel Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 framework governs Li-ion and EV batteries, with recovery targets progressively rising to 90% for portable/EV batteries. CPCB sets an EPR certificate price floor/ceiling (30%-100% of environmental compensation), aiming to formalise a historically fraudulent, paper-only compliance market. India is entirely import-dependent for lithium and cobalt and 75-80% import-dependent for nickel and rare earths — making domestic e-waste/battery recycling a national-security-linked critical-minerals strategy, reinforced by a June 2025 government incentive (reported variously as INR 1,500 crore / USD 180 million) for lithium and rare-earth recovery under the National Critical Mineral Mission.

## Headwinds and tailwinds
Key headwinds include the deep-rooted informal sector offering higher cash prices than formal recyclers can match, fragmented collection infrastructure outside metros, GST differentials (5% on procurement vs 18% on recovered scrap sale) squeezing formal recycler margins, and low consumer awareness (only ~22% of e-waste reaches authorised facilities). Tailwinds include rising global prices for gold/silver/palladium improving recycling economics, growing EV/battery end-of-life volumes from 2028-2030 onward, EPR enforcement tightening (CPCB intensified audits from February 2025), and investor interest in e-waste as a 'critical minerals' and circular-economy theme (e.g., Recyclekaro's USD 7.32 million raise, Attero's ~100% YoY revenue growth claims).

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India's e-waste management market was valued at USD 1.88 billion in 2025, according to Mordor Intelligence, and is expected to grow at around 7.32% a year through 2031; other estimates using a broader market scope put growth as high as 11.59% a year through 2034. Mordor's figures show the market at USD 2.96 billion in 2024, dipping to USD 1.88 billion in 2025, and rising again to USD 2.02 billion in 2026, reflecting how sensitive these estimates are to methodology.

India is the world's third-largest generator of e-waste after China and the US, producing an estimated 3.8 to 6.2 million tonnes a year. Despite this scale, the informal sector still handles the large majority of this volume, recovering far less material value than formal, CPCB-authorised recyclers. Metals make up under 2% of e-waste by weight but drive over 80% of recycler revenue, making metal recovery economics the real engine of the industry.

The core policy lever is Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, which is pushing collection targets higher and widening the range of products covered. Formal recycling capacity has roughly doubled since 2021, but reported recycling-rate improvements are contested, with independent estimates suggesting the true formal share of e-waste processed is still well below official figures.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: Mordor Intelligence values India's e-waste management market at USD 1.88 billion in 2025, projected to reach USD 2.02 billion in 2026 and grow at roughly 7.32% a year through 2031. The same data shows the market was larger in 2024 at USD 2.96 billion and smaller still further back, at USD 1.92 billion in 2020, underlining how estimates vary significantly by year and methodology rather than following a smooth trend line.

Other estimates frame growth more aggressively: IMARC-based projections put the CAGR at 11.59% for 2026-2034, reflecting a broader market scope. Regardless of methodology, the market is expected to keep expanding on the back of EPR compliance escalation, battery-waste growth and rising investor interest in recoverable metals.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: By material type, metal leads with a 46.0% share in 2025, reflecting the high economic value of recovering gold, silver, copper and aluminium. Plastic is the second-largest material at 28.4%, followed by glass at 15.2% (mostly from CRT TVs and monitors) and other materials, including rubber, ceramics and rare-earth-bearing components, at 10.4%.

By source, consumer electronics dominate at 38.0%, driven by smartphone penetration and shorter replacement cycles. Industrial electronics follow at 34.6% and are the fastest-growing source category, while other sources such as medical equipment, industrial machinery and automotive electronics make up 27.4%.

By end-use application, recycling leads with a 50.4% share versus trashing. Regionally, West India leads with 29.0% of the market, supported by Maharashtra's electronics manufacturing density and Gujarat's metallurgical clusters. South India follows at 27.3%, powered by the Bengaluru and Hyderabad IT sectors, then North India at 25.8% (Delhi-NCR's IT concentration) and East India at 17.9%, described as an emerging market with growing formal-sector presence.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: Collection starts with households, bulk consumers (government and corporate, roughly 70% of volume), retailers and informal kabadiwalas or scrap dealers. India has only one formal collection point per 4.9 lakh people, compared with Germany's 45 per lakh, and informal collectors often outbid formal recyclers by offering higher instant cash, pulling material away from the organised chain.

Aggregation and trading happens through informal hubs such as Delhi's Seelampur, Mumbai, Chennai, Bangalore and Kolkata. Delhi is the largest e-waste trading market in the country, with material often funnelling toward Moradabad for metals processing.

Dismantling breaks equipment down into recoverable fractions -- metals, plastics, PCBs, glass. Maharashtra alone has 151 authorised dismantlers versus just 21 recyclers in the state, showing dismantling capacity far exceeds downstream recycling capacity. Dismantling margins are thin, with most value captured further downstream.

Recycling and metal extraction use hydrometallurgical, pyrometallurgical or mechanical processes to recover gold, silver, copper, aluminium and plastics; some PCB material is still exported to overseas smelters where domestic processing capability is lacking. Precious metals supply over 80% of recycler revenue from under 2% of e-waste mass, making this stage the central economic driver of the whole chain. Non-recoverable hazardous residues, such as glass scrap, PCB dust and flue-gas cleaning residue, are sent to Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities.

sections.heading: Distribution & channels
prose: Most of India's e-waste still flows through informal channels. Informal operators -- kabadiwalas, scrap dealers and local aggregators -- handle an estimated 60-70% of volume. Only 10% goes to Grade A (authorised) recyclers and 6% to Grade B (authorised dismantlers), while 10-15% sits unrecycled at home and 8-10% ends up in landfill.
This split means roughly 70% of consumer e-waste bypasses the formal, CPCB-authorised system entirely, limiting the volume available to organised recyclers despite their higher recovery efficiency.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: Attero Recycling is the clear market leader, commanding an estimated 25% of India's organised e-waste sector -- the most commercially dominant single-company position in the industry. It operates hydrometallurgical e-waste and battery recycling with around 45 patents, copper purity above 99.95%, FY24 revenue of about INR 446 crore, and claims roughly 100% year-on-year revenue growth heading toward FY26 revenue near INR 2,000 crore.

Behind Attero, a group of strong challengers includes Eco Recycling Ltd (Ecoreco), which expanded its processing capacity to 31,200 MTPA in July 2025 with a new plant at Vasai; Cerebra Integrated Technologies, which runs a 90,000-tonne annual capacity plant in Bengaluru; and Re Sustainability (Ramky Enviro Engineers), which is piloting decentralised micro-plants in Tier-2 cities to cut reverse-logistics costs.

Namo eWaste Management had an oversubscribed NSE SME listing in September 2024 at a 90% premium and commissioned a 12,240 MTPA lithium-ion battery recycling plant in Nashik in July 2025. RecycleKaro positions itself as India's largest end-to-end lithium-ion battery recycler and one of the largest CPCB-authorised e-waste processors, having launched India's first Plasma Furnace Technology unit in March 2024 (targeting 75,000 MT/annum) and a digital platform, ReLoop, in June 2025.

Other notable players include Exigo Recycling (2 plants in Haryana covering 100+ cities), TES-AMM India (3 plants across Karnataka, Telangana and Haryana), E-Parisaraa (one of India's first CPCB-approved recyclers since 2004, with clients including IBM, Tata Elxsi, ABB and Philips), Earth Sense Recycling (5 plants across five states), and Karo Sambhav, the only Indian Producer Responsibility Organization in the global WEEE Forum, with clients including Apple, Cisco, Dell, Flipkart, HP, Lenovo and Nokia (HMD). Hulladek Recycling runs a Kolkata-based 'urban mining' collection model, Antony Waste Handling Cell expanded its commercial footprint by 28% in 2025 through municipal concessions, and Recykal, a digital EPR trading and e-waste marketplace, raised a USD 22 million Series B in 2025 to extend to 180 cities. Despite this roster, the market overall remains fragmented, with the top five firms controlling well under 20% of total industry revenue.

sections.heading: Margins
prose: Metal recovery dominates recycler economics: precious and base metals contribute about 46% of material value by type but drive over 80% of recycler revenue despite being under 2% of e-waste mass. This concentration means formal recyclers' profitability depends heavily on access to metal-rich waste streams rather than the bulk of plastic or glass material they process.

A tax mismatch squeezes formal recycler margins: formal operators pay only 5% GST on procuring end-of-life electrical and electronic equipment, but are charged 18% GST when selling recovered scrap metals. This 13-point GST differential raises costs for compliant, tax-paying formal recyclers while informal operators, who evade taxation entirely, face no equivalent burden.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: India's formal, authorised e-waste recycling capacity stood at 1.8 million tonnes per year as of 2024, with 595 authorised recyclers operating across 22 states. Despite this scale, capacity utilisation is estimated at only around 10%, meaning most installed formal capacity sits idle because too little e-waste is actually routed into the formal system.

Among individual players, Attero Recycling's plants (Roorkee and others) have a combined capacity of 150,000 tonnes per year, Cerebra Integrated Technologies runs a 90,000-tonne-per-year plant in Bengaluru, RecycleKaro's Plasma Furnace unit targets 75,000 tonnes per year, and Eco Recycling Ltd's Vasai facility adds 31,200 tonnes per year.

On the trade side, India is a signatory to the Basel Convention, and e-waste imports are formally prohibited under Annex VIII A1180, though loopholes such as donation claims and used-EEE-for-recycling provisions have historically allowed inflows -- estimated at around 50,000 tonnes in both 2007 and 2009. The E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 now require importers of used EEE to take on 100% EPR responsibility for equipment that reaches end-of-life and is not re-exported. GST on e-waste was cut from 28% to 5% to support formal recycling economics, though the gap with the 18% GST on recovered scrap sales continues to squeeze formal recycler margins.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: Several factors support growth. Advanced hydrometallurgical processing now enables up to 98% precious-metal recovery rates, improving unit economics for formal recyclers. Investor appetite is rising, with venture capital and private equity increasingly viewing e-waste and battery recycling as a circular-economy and critical-minerals investment theme -- illustrated by Recyclekaro's USD 7.32 million raise and Namo eWaste's oversubscribed NSE SME listing. CPCB registration becoming mandatory is expected to formalise the organised sector and curb unorganised dumping, and India's recoverable e-waste resources were estimated at around USD 6 billion in economic potential in FY24 from metal extraction alone.

Headwinds remain significant. The informal sector handles 60-90%-plus of e-waste at far lower recovery efficiency -- just 10-20% material recovery versus 95-97% in formal facilities -- diverting value from organised recyclers and creating environmental and health hazards. An 18% GST on recovered scrap metals, against only 5% GST paid on procuring end-of-life EEE, erodes formal recycler margins while informal operators evade taxation entirely.

India is also heavily import-dependent on the very critical minerals -- lithium, cobalt, rare earths, and 90% of copper -- that e-waste recycling could help supply domestically, leaving the country exposed to China's dominance of rare-earth supply and pricing. Fraudulent EPR certification by spurious or non-operational recyclers distorts the market, prompting intensified CPCB audits from February 2025. The E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 cover only four metals (copper, aluminium, iron, gold) under the EPR mandate, despite more than 15 precious and critical minerals carrying substantial recovery value, leaving most material value outside formal regulatory incentives. Finally, illegal e-waste imports from developed countries persist despite Basel Convention membership and import bans, straining already-overloaded informal hubs like Moradabad and Seelampur.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's e-waste management market is set to keep growing at a double-digit-to-high-single-digit pace, with Mordor Intelligence projecting roughly 7.32% annual growth from 2026 through 2031 and IMARC-based estimates suggesting as much as 11.59% through 2034. Growth will be driven by rising EPR collection targets (60% in FY2023-24 rising to 80% by FY2027-28) across an expanded 106 EEE product categories, the build-out of battery and critical-minerals recycling as lithium-ion battery waste is projected to grow 6x by 2030 and 50x by 2035 versus 2025 levels, and continued government support such as the June 2025 incentive for critical-minerals recycling under the National Critical Mineral Mission.

The main constraint on this growth is structural: the informal sector's continued dominance of collection, the GST mismatch that squeezes formal recycler margins, and EPR rules that still only formally incentivise recovery of four metals. Unless formal collection infrastructure, tax treatment and regulatory coverage of critical minerals improve, a large share of India's e-waste value will keep flowing through informal channels even as the overall market expands.

value_chain.margin_note: Delhi is the largest e-waste trading market in India; material funnels toward Moradabad for metals processing.

value_chain.description: Dismantlers break down equipment into recoverable fractions (metals, plastics, PCBs, glass); Maharashtra alone has 151 authorised dismantlers.

value_chain.description: Formal recyclers use hydrometallurgical, pyrometallurgical or mechanical processes to extract gold, silver, copper, aluminium and plastics; some PCB material is still exported to overseas smelters when domestic metals-processing capability is lacking.

margins.notes: Attero's FY24 financials: revenue INR 446 crore, gross margin ~23%, EBITDA margin ~8%, with EPR revenue contributing ~20% of total revenue. EPR fees contribute 25-30% of recyclers' revenue industry-wide but irregular billing cycles create working capital challenges. Precious metals supply over 80% of recycling revenue for advanced facilities from under 2% of e-waste mass; hydrometallurgical refiners achieve 93% copper and near-100% precious metal recovery. An 18% GST on recovered scrap metals (vs 5% GST on procurement) erodes formal recycler margins relative to tax-evading informal players.

duty.note: India is a signatory to the Basel Convention; e-waste import is prohibited under Annex VIII A1180, though loopholes (donation claims, used-EEE-for-recycling provisions) have historically allowed inflows.
E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 require importers of used EEE to assume 100% EPR responsibility for end-of-life equipment not re-exported.
GST on e-waste reduced from 28% to 5% to support formal recycling economics, but a 13-point differential vs the 18% GST on recovered scrap sales still squeezes formal recycler margins.

source.snippet: 595 authorised recyclers operate across 22 states
